children: If you've spent time looking at a price chart, you've probably noticed something curious. Prices don't move in straight lines. They tend to stall, bounce, or reverse at certain price levels repeatedly, almost as if there's an invisible floor or ceiling. That's not a coincidence. It's one of the oldest and most reliable concepts in technical analysis: support and resistance.
Whether you trade stocks, forex, crypto, or commodities, understanding support and resistance is often the first real skill that separates someone reading charts from someone who understands them.
Here's how support and resistance work and how traders use them:
What are support and resistance?

Support is a price level where a downtrend tends to pause or reverse because buying interest becomes strong enough to overcome selling pressure. Think of it as a "floor" that the price has trouble falling through.

Resistance is the opposite. It is a price level where an uptrend tends to stall or reverse because selling pressure overwhelms buying interest. It acts like a "ceiling" that the price struggles to break above.

Example : In the chart below, Siemens' stock traded between Rs 3,300 and Rs 4,200 over the past six months. Every time it drops toward Rs 3,300, buyers step in and push it back up. Every time it rallies toward Rs 4,150-4,200, sellers step in and push it back down. In this case, Rs 3,300 is acting as support and Rs 4,150-4,200 is acting as resistance. The stock is essentially range-bound between the two, as shown below.
Why do these levels exist?
Support and resistance aren't magic lines drawn by fate they're a reflection of collective human psychology.
Market psychology: Traders remember key price levels, making them self-reinforcing.
Supply & demand: Buyers defend support, while sellers dominate resistance.
Psychological levels: Round numbers often act as key price zones.
Institutional activity: Large orders are commonly placed near important levels.
Order clustering: Stop-losses and targets around these levels can trigger sharp breakouts or breakdowns.
Role Reversal: When support becomes resistance (and vice versa)

One of the most useful concepts in this whole topic is that broken support often becomes the new resistance, while broken resistance often becomes the new support. This phenomenon is known as "polarity flipping."
Here's logic

: If a price level held as support for some time and then finally breaks down, many traders who bought at that level are now sitting on losses. When the price eventually rallies back to that old support level, those traders may sell just to break even, turning what was once a floor into a new ceiling. The reverse also happens when resistance breaks and becomes support on a pullback.

Example: One 97 Communications (Paytm) has struggled to close above Rs 1,250-1,270. That's resistance. It finally breaks out, trading up to Rs 1,400, before pulling back to Rs 1,290 and bouncing higher again. In this case, the old resistance at Rs 1,250-1,270 has become new support. A trader using this pattern might have waited for that pullback to Rs 1,290 as their entry point, rather than chasing the initial breakout at Rs 1,400.

Ultimately, support and resistance provide a framework for understanding price behaviour and identifying potential trading opportunities. While they are not guarantees of future price movements, using these levels alongside other technical indicators can help traders make more informed and disciplined decisions.
